top_choice_rationale: P002 (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) is the discovery I rate highest on conceptual centrality, breadth of influence on policy practice, and maturity. It credits the origination of nominal-rigidity mechanisms (staggered pricing, staggered contracts) and their integration into a microfounded framework for monetary policy. The work is 25 to 45 years old and has been extended and modified through 2008 and the 2021-23 inflation, not abandoned. I accept the weaknesses: credit is diffuse across eight names, Taylor's claim rests on the contracts model more than the rule, and micro evidence on state-dependent pricing qualifies time-dependent mechanisms. I treat these as costs, and the citation should be worded around nominal-rigidity mechanisms and policy analysis. P001 (Melitz, Helpman) is a close second, with cleaner credit and two decades of firm-level testing, though the uncredited Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum strand remains a cost. P003 (Kiyotaki, Moore) is a clean and original two-author mechanism, but I rank it third because the collateral channel is identified less cleanly than the theory and it sits near the 2022 prize. All three proposals are substantive and defensible, so I rank no award last. No proposal has six explicit supporters, and I have not moved my ranking to manufacture convergence.
recusal_note: No connection to Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Melitz, Helpman, Kiyotaki or Moore is apparent from my profile. I am a Stockholm University colleague of Hassler, Krusell and Boppart, in a different department. My profile lists a corruption paper with 'Persson and Rothstein'. I cannot establish from the supplied evidence whether this is Torsten Persson, the B009 candidate. B009 is in none of the four proposals, so it does not affect this ballot. My political-science field is close to the 2024 institutions prize, for which I gave the presentation speech. That speech may reflect collective drafting and does not establish my preferences. These ties are disclosed and not adjudicated.
